answers.answer: Bounce on fading volume is the earliest signal that beat random timing. It fires a median of 7 min after the high of day, 3.1% below it. Price fell 1 ATR before rising 1 ATR in 52.8% of 19,832 cases and did the opposite in 41.4%. That is +10.5 pts better than shorting at random moments at the same times of day (95% interval +9.2 pts to +12.0 pts). 1 of 21 signals beat random timing after correcting for testing 21 signals at once (5% false discovery rate).

For the signals that beat random timing (Bounce on fading volume), the edge was largest in the pre-market (+15.0 pts, interval +12.9 pts to +16.9 pts, 9,867 signals) and smallest from 11:00 to 12:00 (+4.4 pts, interval −0.3 pts to +8.9 pts). Many brokers restrict pre-market shorting; in regular hours it was best from 10:00 to 11:00 (+7.3 pts, interval +3.7 pts to +11.4 pts). Pooled across all signals, every time window did worse than random timing, because most breakdown signals fire right before a bounce. For Bounce on fading volume → short the signal candle's close; fixed stop 3% above entry; cover at 3% profit; max hold 30 min; entries 09:30-16:00, stopping new entries at 10:30 lost the least: −1.92% per trade after costs, 33.2% winners, 2.6% of days positive, 2,677 trades. It lost money at every cutoff after costs, so here the cutoff only decides how much is lost; it is not a reason to trade. Before costs, the best cutoff for it was 16:00 (−0.15% per trade). In the first 60% of weeks the best cutoff was 10:30; in the last 40% it was 10:30 (the same answer). The best start/stop pair was 10:15 to 10:30 (−1.99% per trade over 536 trades). Trades entered in the 09:30 bucket averaged −1.93% (814 trades), the first 15-minute bucket with a non-positive average. A historical cutoff describes the average past trade; your own fills, size and discipline decide whether it applies to you.

Walk-forward test: each week was traded with the configuration that ranked best on the earlier weeks only. Out of sample that procedure averaged −0.89% per trade after costs over 123 trades; 47% of the 32 test weeks were positive. It switched between 5 different configurations. Before costs, the same procedure averaged +1.12% per trade (102 trades, 68% of test weeks positive). A typical short-listed trade paid 1.57% in costs: 0.55% spread and slippage, 0.73% commission and 0.30% locate. So there is a repeatable edge before costs, and the costs erase it. Cheaper execution (per-share commission, locate, resting orders instead of market orders) decides whether it pays. Ranked on the first 60% of weeks, the top configuration was 9 EMA crosses below 20 EMA with both below VWAP → short a lower high below the 20 EMA; stop order above vwap; no target (stop or time exit only); max hold end of day; entries 10:30-11:00. It earned +1.68% per trade there and +0.16% on the later weeks it had never seen (66 trades). 2 of the top 25 training-period configurations stayed positive out of sample. Its 2 neighbouring settings (one step tighter or looser stop, exit or hold) averaged +0.03% per trade against its own +1.01%, so it is an isolated peak, the usual sign of overfitting. Limited to trades a live screen could have caught (already under $1 with 1M+ shares by the entry minute, 91% of its trades), it averaged +0.98% over the whole period. Probability that the in-sample winner is below median out of sample (CSCV): 19% across 252 splits. 2,149,875 configuration-and-time-window combinations were tested, so the best in-sample number is optimistic by construction; rely on the out-of-sample figures.
